doc.title: Joe Muranyi interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 11, 2007

chapter: Childhood in Ohio and first music
title: Accordion and violin lessons, father's wish for an electrician
summary: Early lessons on accordion and violin fizzled out, and his father wanted him to become a union electrician.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: Were your parents wanting you to get a trade, a craft that would make a nice life for you?

Well that develops — I was going to take accordion lessons from my father — not my father, a friend of my father’s, some Italian guy. And I never got to handle an accordion ever, and I took lessons for three or four months. It was all solfeggio on a grand scale and
all of that, you know, it was like I’m dying to get my hands on something. So I don’t know what happened.
Oh you mean you were taking lessons and you never even got to play one for a while.

Yeah, yeah, yeah. I don’t remember if I had solfeggio or singing, maybe, but it was grand staff, the do-re-me-fa-so-la-C and all that kind of stuff, and I guess I sort of forgot it because — I don’t know, maybe it had some early — and then I was going to take violin lessons. There was a guy named Pragia who came from Cleveland. And I don’t think he was a gypsy, he was just sort of a very artistic, very, a fairly young guy with pale skin and very delicate fingers and was a hell of a violin player. And I had like one lesson or something or two lessons, and he was letting me hold it and things like that, and he stopped coming to Martin’s Ferry. I think he had like a route he’d do, he’d come and teach the Hungarian community, and he’d teach kids. So he disappeared so that was that. So they wanted a musical education for me, they didn’t want me to be a musician particularly. They were good parents. My father wasn’t a drunk or you know, like he was a respectable family man, he had to provide for his family. And later on when I was a teenager he wanted me to be an electrician. He had a friend that was an electrician in the union and he could have gotten me into the union at age 17 or 18 or whatever like that, which is like guaranteeing you a lifetime income you know. And I wasn’t interested, no I was interested in music, and that didn’t appeal to me you know. Idiot. I always wondered what would have happened had I done it. I think I still would have been musical you know. As a young musician’s life, as we all know, is not the most secure in general.
